idiom_name: PORO mapper methods (from_hash / to_h) with Data.define boundary value objects
implementation_notes: Ruby's idiom is a plain object or module with two methods - `UserMapper.from_hash(payload)` and `UserMapper.to_hash(user)` - plus `Data.define` (or Struct) for the boundary value object, whose core `members` and `to_h` support makes the mechanical half free: `UserPayload.new(**h.slice(*UserPayload.members))` for the untranslated fields. Keep the mapper in its own file so only it knows both the payload keys and the domain attributes, and prefer Data over Struct for boundary values because Data instances are frozen by construction. dry-struct + dry-transformer (or ROM, which started as 'Ruby Object Mapper') provide a declarative version of the same layer when many shapes and coercions must be declared rather than coded; for one pair of shapes the PORO is shorter and dependency-free.
code_sketch:
UserPayload = Data.define(:id, :full_name, :admin)   # frozen boundary value

module UserMapper                                     # both directions, one place
  def self.from_hash(h) = User.new(id: h.fetch("id"),
                                   full_name: h.fetch("full_name"),
                                   admin: h.fetch("admin", false))
  def self.to_hash(u)   = { "id" => u.id, "full_name" => u.full_name }
end
pitfalls: Hash keys are untyped: reading `h[:id]` when the payload carries "id" yields nil and the mapper builds a silently broken object - normalise keys once and use `fetch` for required fields.
Struct and Data members are both positional and keyword: mixing `Data.define(:a, :b)` with positional construction in one place invites silent argument-order bugs.
`to_hash` output aliases nested mutable values unless duplicated, so a later mutation of the domain object changes the payload already considered 'mapped'.
Monkey-patching `to_h` onto domain classes moves the mapping into the model and destroys the isolation the mapper exists to provide.
